The AI tax nobody is talking about: Intelligence Exhaust.

Imagine hiring a consultant.

They spend weeks shadowing your best employees.

They learn your workflows.

They understand your customers.

They document your competitive edge.

The project ends.

Six months later...

They package everything they learned into a product and start selling it to your competitors.

You didn't just pay for consulting.

You paid to train your future competitor.

Welcome to the AI economy.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently called this the Reverse Information Paradox.

Historically, sellers worried buyers would copy their information.

Now, buyers voluntarily hand over their proprietary knowledge to make AI useful.

Every prompt.

Every correction.

Every workflow.

Every document uploaded.

Every "No, that's not how our business works."

That's intelligence exhaust.

Now add Jevons Paradox to the mix.

Jevons observed that when something becomes more efficient, we don't use less of it.

We use more.

AI has made knowledge work dramatically cheaper.

So what do we do?

More code.
More contracts.
More customer conversations.
More product strategies.
More internal documentation.
More institutional knowledge.

The better AI gets...

The more we feed it.

But here's the part that should make every enterprise pause.

AI companies are no longer just technology vendors.

They're becoming businesses in their own right.

Look at what's happening.

Coding assistants are evolving into full software engineering platforms.
AI search is competing with traditional search engines.
AI assistants are becoming researchers, analysts and consultants.
AI customer service agents are replacing traditional support providers.
Foundation model companies are building productivity suites, enterprise search, legal assistants, healthcare copilots, financial advisors and cybersecurity tools.

Today's AI supplier could become tomorrow's competitor.

And what fuels these products?

Millions of interactions.

Millions of prompts.

Millions of enterprise workflows.

Your proprietary knowledge isn't just making your organization more productive.

It could also be helping build the next product that competes with yours.

This doesn't mean we should stop adopting AI.

Far from it.

It means AI governance is no longer just about security, privacy and compliance.

It's about protecting organizational intelligence.

The question every leadership team should be asking is:

"What knowledge should never leave our walls?"

Perhaps the biggest AI tax isn't the subscription fee.

It's the expertise we're unknowingly contributing to someone else's competitive advantage.

What are your thoughts?

Is "Intelligence Exhaust" a real strategic risk, or simply the inevitable price of AI-driven innovation?

#AI #GenerativeAI #EnterpriseAI #TechLeadership #BusinessStrategy #KnowledgeManagement #DigitalTransformation #JevonsParadox

SOAP vs REST in the AI Era: Is SOAP Still Relevant?


With AI generating API code, XML payloads, and integration templates in seconds, a question often comes up:
Is SOAP becoming obsolete?
My answer is No.
AI is changing how we build integrations, not which API we should choose.
Here's how I think about it.
🔹 Choose SOAP when you need:
✅ Business process execution
✅ Rich enterprise operations
✅ Strongly typed contracts (WSDL)
✅ Mature enterprise integrations
Examples include hiring, staffing changes, worker updates, and payroll related operations.
🔹 Choose REST when you need:
✅ Lightweight integrations
✅ Faster development
✅ Mobile and web applications
✅ Simple CRUD operations
✅ JSON based communication
REST is ideal for modern applications that prioritize speed and simplicity.
Where AI fits in
AI doesn't replace either API.
Instead, it helps developers work more efficiently by:
🤖 Explaining WSDL operations
🤖 Generating SOAP request XML
🤖 Creating REST request examples
🤖 Interpreting SOAP Faults and HTTP errors
🤖 Writing test payloads
🤖 Explaining complex XML or JSON responses
The developer still validates the solution, but AI can significantly reduce research and development time.
My rule of thumb
📌 Need to execute complex Workday business processes?
➡️ SOAP
📌 Need fast, lightweight data exchange?
➡️ REST
📌 Need to develop faster?
➡️ Use AI as your development assistant, regardless of which API you choose.
My biggest takeaway
The future isn't SOAP vs REST.
It's SOAP + REST + AI, where each plays a different role.
Understanding when to use each technology is becoming a more valuable skill than simply knowing how to write an API request.
If you were starting a new Workday integration today, would you choose SOAP, REST, or a combination of both? Why?
